SEC-HD-01.note: KEY PROBLEM. D 'drifted steadily out of date in the thirty years since the last of those librarians retired' is defensible. The author's doubt is well founded: simple past with a durational 'in the N years since X' adverbial occurs in edited prose ('the city changed a lot in the ten years since I left') and is not ungrammatical. Crucially D fails no OTHER test - it is number-neutral, so tense is the sole discriminator, and that discriminator is contested. B is the better answer, not the only one. Recommend rewriting D (e.g. give it a wrong number or a clashing time adverbial) or dropping the item; as written it is the same failure mode as the 'had already showed' loss.

SEC-HD-02.note: 'by the time X begins' + anteriority forces the future perfect. B 'will go' places the thaw at the boundary rather than before it; C is a present perfect in a future frame; D is counterfactual. Only B is even a contender, and it loses cleanly. Not hard: one rule, one live competitor.

SEC-HD-03.note: Key unique. A 'potters find a glaze' is a fully grammatical sentence in isolation and is rejected only by the attachment of 'Fired... and buried...', which is exactly the second-feature structure that makes an item hard. D is doubly wrong (misattached + singular subject clashing with the later 'no two of them'). B supplies no finite verb. Genuinely hard.

SEC-HD-04.note: Author's doubt checked and rejected. The notional-unity exception to plural agreement ('bread and butter is') is limited to conventionalised pairs under a single determiner; three fully articulated gerund-participial clauses, each with its own object, coordinate to a plural subject. The framing sentence ('Restoring a wetland is not the same thing...') invites a unitary reading but does not license 'takes'. Medium rather than hard: the proximity trap ('a standing budget') is the only pull, and D/C are on-sight rejects.

SEC-HD-05.note: 'those' is required for the plural 'budgets'; A's 'that of' is a frequent error but not a defensible variant in edited prose when the antecedent is overtly plural and adjacent. C's double possessive ('of a ... seal's') and B's category mismatch (budgets vs animals) are both visible without the sentence. Downgraded from the file's 'hard': only A is live, and the number match is a single step.

SEC-HD-06.note: Author's doubt checked. B 'would have damped out ... by the drag of air' is wrong by rule, not merely odd: 'damp out' here is intransitive/unaccusative, and English does not license a causer 'by'-phrase on an active unaccusative (cf. *'the balloon rose by the heat'). The 'by' phrase is fixed passage text, so it selects the passive. C and D fail the past counterfactual. Key unique; this is nevertheless the item whose distractor sits closest to the line, because a solver who reads 'by' as instrumental could talk themselves into B.

SEC-HD-07.note: 'not so much' admits only 'as'. A ('than') and B/D ('but') import the second halves of other correlatives. D additionally breaks the prepositional-phrase parallel. Single closed rule with one legal completion, so medium at best for a student who knows the correlative and near-impossible for one who does not - which is not the same thing as hard.

SEC-HD-08.note: Three-item predicate series with two finite past verbs already set; A matches. C 'would list' is not ungrammatical in isolation and is rejected on tense/aspect consistency plus the following 'names that appear nowhere' - slightly softer than the explanation implies, but the series parallel is decisive. B is the standard -ing throwaway.

SEC-HD-09.note: Key unique: the pronoun is the object of 'of', so 'whom' regardless of the phrase's later subject role - this even sidesteps the contested 'who(m) I thought was' dispute, since the case is fixed by the preposition, not by the embedded clause. 'which' is blocked by animacy, 'them' produces a run-on. Hard because the pull toward 'who' comes from the pronoun's apparent subjecthood in 'would read'. passage_needed false: 'most of whom' is the only always-legal option in the set, so a blind solver takes it by convention. Minor infelicity in the stem: a non-restrictive 'most of whom' relative would normally take a comma after 'servants'; consider adding one.

SEC-HD-10.note: Author's prediction confirmed: three on-sight rejects. A colon after 'including' and after 'are' are both flat errors visible without reading the sentence, and the semicolon-before-a-list is a stock reject. The bare colon is the only clean option in the set, so this is solvable blind. Easy.

SEC-HD-11.note: Author's prediction confirmed. B and C leave a fragment after the participial opener and are rejected without reading anything; that leaves a bare singular/plural coin-flip that the passage settles ('them', 'one of them'). One feature, two live options. Easy.

SEC-HD-12.note: Series whose items carry internal commas is separated by semicolons and the last item keeps its conjunction: '; and'. B is the only real competitor and fails on consistency with the semicolon already standing after 'arsenal'. D's 'while' cannot coordinate a noun phrase into the series. Medium.

SEC-HD-13.note: Author's doubt checked and rejected. An appositive never governs agreement; 'a pairing' re-describes the compound subject and leaves the verb answering to 'The list itself and the culture', which is plural. 'together' and the closing 'either one on its own' both confirm two entities. A is a strong trap but not defensible. Hard by the intended definition: C gets the number right and fails only on the present-tense frame set by 'look alike', 'work differently', 'changes'.

SEC-HD-14.note: Author's prediction confirmed. 'every' + plural and the stray possessive are both on-sight rejects; what remains is one comma in a visibly parallel three-item series. Easy.

SEC-HD-15.note: Key unique. An open parenthesis cannot be closed by a comma or left open, which kills B and C at a glance; D closes it correctly and then strands 'The plant dyes' with no predicate. Downgraded from the file's 'hard': the missing-main-verb check on D is a familiar move and only one option survives the paren rule alongside it.

SEC-HD-16.note: Key unique, and the item is saved by its second feature. The mandative subjunctive alone would leave A arguable, since British edited usage tolerates the indicative after 'require that'; but the later alternative is the bare 'react', and 'requires that the cacher models ... rather than react' cannot be made parallel. So the parallel, not the subjunctive, is what makes A uniquely wrong. Hard, and correctly built.

SEC-HD-17.note: Proximity agreement under 'either ... or' with an intervening relative clause; the key is the plural 'trip' after the nearer plural 'relays'. A is the designed trap (agreeing with the distant singular), C reverses both, D adds an unlicensed subject-verb comma. Hard on the rule. passage_needed false only because the options carry their own subjects, so a blind solver can pick the internally consistent uncomma'd pair without the 'either ... or' frame - a structural leak, not a defect in the key.

SEC-HD-18.note: Key unique: the participial opener 'Sinking more easily on the descent' must be followed by the bird as subject. But all three distractors are wrong for the SAME single reason - each demotes the cormorant out of subject position - so there is no second feature to settle and a student who applies the attachment rule once gets it. Medium, not hard. (Note: the brief's HD-18 doubt describes 'had already grown soft' vs 'had already been softened', which is SEC-HD-23, not this item; see that entry.)

SEC-HD-19.note: 'along with' is a supplement, not a coordinator, so the verb answers to the plural 'The maps' across ~25 words of intervening material. A is doubly wrong (number + unclosed supplement), B is the pure agreement trap, D punctuates correctly and leaves no finite verb. Hard: the distance plus the two adjacent singular nouns make 'comes' feel right, and the punctuation is a genuine second feature.

SEC-HD-20.note: Comma after a fronted dependent clause, and no comma between 'patterns' and 'show'. Two features, but both are stock and A's semicolon-with-a-dependent-clause-on-its-left is an on-sight reject. Medium.

SEC-HD-21.note: Key unique: fronted 'Not only' requires subject-auxiliary inversion, and 'do' agrees with the compound plural subject; 'have ... live' cannot take a bare infinitive. Downgraded from 'hard' and passage_needed set false for the same reason: the compound subject sits inside the options themselves, so both the inversion and the agreement are decidable from the option text without the sentence. This is the most options-solvable item in the batch.

SEC-HD-22.note: Paired commas around the state name, and no comma splitting the compound predicate 'opened ... and closed'. Genuinely two features, but both rules are common currency and B (which gets the state right and then splits the predicate) is the only real competitor. Medium.

SEC-HD-23.note: This is the item the brief's HD-18 doubt describes, and the doubt does not bite: the passage DOES supply the agent ('by crews who had no reason to think it mattered'), and that phrase is fixed stem text, not part of any option. With A 'had already grown soft', the by-phrase has nothing to attach to and the crews fall out of the sentence, so A is ungrammatical in situ despite carrying the right tense. B is in the wrong frame under 'By the time the final splice was made'; D is imperfective and also cannot host the agent. Key unique; hard, and this is the batch's cleanest tense-plus-voice item.

SEC-HD-24.note: Singular 'difference' with 'between the two' as an attractor. A and D fail on number, C is the -ing throwaway, and D would additionally break the present frame. One live trap, one step. Medium.
